Steady-State Voltage Profile Analysis in Radial Low-Voltage Feeders with Rooftop Photovoltaic Systems (2013, conference, Proceedings of the International Symposium on Industrial Electronics and Applications, Osijek).
Authors: Aleksandar Jeremić (R0696); Dragan Vuković (outside co-author); Miroslav Stanić (outside co-author).
Keywords: voltage profile; radial feeder; backward-forward sweep; photovoltaic; EN 50160.
This paper presents a steady-state power flow analysis of a 0.4 kV radial distribution feeder in an urban residential area of Novi Sad, incorporating measured generation profiles from twelve rooftop photovoltaic installations aggregating 48 kWp of installed capacity. A backward–forward sweep load flow algorithm was implemented and validated against one week of SCADA measurements. Voltage profiles were computed under three penetration scenarios: 20 %, 50 %, and 80 % of feeder customers operating as prosumers. Results indicate that reverse power flow emerges at penetration levels above 35 % under peak irradiance conditions, causing end-of-feeder voltage to exceed the EN 50160 upper limit of 1.10 p.u. for approximately 4.2 % of annual hours at 80 % penetration. The sensitivity of voltage rise to feeder impedance ratio X/R was quantified, showing that resistive-dominant cables characteristic of low-voltage grids amplify voltage deviations by a factor of 1.6 compared to equivalent medium-voltage lines. The study provides a benchmark dataset and simulation framework subsequently used in follow-up hosting capacity work.

Characterisation of PV output variability and its effect on demand-peak coincidence in a small industrial park (2019, conference, Solar and Renewable Energy Proceedings – Southeast Europe).
Authors: Александра Ковачевић (R0681); Nataša Petrović (outside co-author); Bojan Filipović (outside co-author).
Keywords: PV variability; demand peak; irradiance; industrial park; load shifting.
Measured one-minute irradiance and PV output data from three rooftop arrays (7, 11 and 18 kWp) installed at an industrial park in Novi Sad were analysed over two full calendar years (2018–2019) to characterise output variability and its statistical relationship to afternoon demand peaks. The variability index, defined as the standard deviation of one-minute ramp rates normalised by rated capacity, averaged 0.031 min⁻¹ in summer and 0.058 min⁻¹ in winter. Cross-correlation between aggregated PV output and the grid demand peaks billed under the local distribution tariff showed that PV generation offset the dominant peak-demand interval on only 38% of weekdays in summer, because afternoon storms regularly suppress generation during peak hours. The findings suggest that demand-peak reduction through PV alone is unreliable without coordinated load-shifting of deferrable loads such as compressors and chillers.
